rabbi-yochanan-b-napacha.bio: R. Yochanan studied under R. Yehudah haNasi and emerged as the next leader after his death. He directed the academy in Tiberias and set up the groundwork for the Jerusalem Talmud. His unusual beauty, sharpness and personal sufferings made him a captivating yet intimidating teacher. It was due to his personality and his unrivaled learning that the center of Torah study did not move to Babylonia during his lifetime.

rabbi-yose-b-chalafta.bio: R. Yose b. Chalafta learned from many teachers but was a disciple of R. Akiva. Preserving many traditions from his father, he served as an authority in transmitting them to his younger contemporaries. He is credited with the compilation of Seder Olam, the classical compendium of traditional history.

aliases: Rav Huna, the Head of the Diaspora
rav-huna.bio: Rav Huna, originally a disciple of Rav, later succeeded him as the head of the academy in Sura after a period without a leader. His profound scholarship and the diminishing influence of the center in Palestine prompted the Babylonian community to forge a more autonomous path. However, in financial matters, Rav Huna instructed his students to adhere to the rulings of Rav Nachman.

rabbi-yose-b-chanina.bio: R. Yose b. Chanina was a prominent judge and is frequently cited in the Talmud Yerushalmi. He was one of R. Yochanan's most important students and eventually became one of his colleagues. Appearing in Rabbi Zeira's dream, he reported that his place in the upper realms was directly next to his teacher (Bava Metzia 85b).

rabbi-yose-b-yehudah.bio: R. Yose b. Yehudah was the son of the famed R. Yehudah b. Il'ai, as well as his student. He was often involved in disputes with R. Yehudah haNasi, as well as with scholars of his father's generation.

rabbi-yose-hagelili.bio: R. Yose haGelili was a pious and independent-minded student of R. Akiva. He was prolific and his opinions are frequently cited. Among his many students was R. Elazar b. Azaryah.

rebbi-yose-b-rebbu-abun.bio: R. Yose b. Abun (or Avin or Bun) is one of the names that appears most frequently in the Yerushalmi. He is from the last group of scholars mentioned there by name and is thought to have had a major role in the Yerushalmi's formation. He often cites earlier traditions from Babylonia as well as from the Land of Israel and seeks to clarify them.

rabbah-b-rav-huna.bio: Rabbah b. Rav Huna was the son of head of the academy in Sura. He also studied under the latter's rival, Rav Chisda. He was known as a paradigm of humility.

rabban-yochanan-b-zakkai.bio: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was a first-century Jewish leader and scholar who oversaw the fragile transition of the Jewish people to life without a [Temple](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/beit-hamikdash?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources), upon the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE at the hands of the Romans. While he sought accommodation with the Romans, he was unable to convince the faction of zealots to give up their position, which ultimately led to the destruction of [Jerusalem](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/jerusalem?tab=admin). Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's students smuggled him out of Jerusalem, enabling him to renew Jewish life and learning from [Yavneh](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/yavneh?tab=admin). rabbi-yishmael-b-yose.bio: R. Yishmael b. Yose studied under his father, R. Yose b. Chalafta, and most of his many teachings are stated in the name of his father. He was a friend and study partner of R. Yehudah haNasi. At one point, he controversially worked for the Roman government catching thieves.

rav-hiyya-b-yosef.bio: [Rav] Hiyya b. Yosef was a student of Rav who would exchange Rav's teaching with Shmuel's responses. When Rav died, he studied under Shmuel and then went to Israel, where he taught and studied with R. Yochanan, again bringing the teachings of Rav.

rabbi-elazar-b-yose.bio: R. Elazar b. Yosi is from the later teachers in the Land of Israel. He was a colleague of R. Yose b. Abun.

yose-b-yoezer.bio: Yose b. Yoezer and Yose b. Yochanan served as the first of the zugot (pairs), with the first being Nasi (religious leader) and the second the head of the court. They served after Antigonos in a period of intense Hellenization and war, and promulgated several leniencies to encourage Jews to keep the law under these difficult conditions.

rabbi-yose-b-kippar.bio: R. Yose b. Kippar was a student of R. Elazar b. Shamu'a and was an emissary from the Land of Israel to the ascendant Jewish community in Babylonia.

rav-yosef-b-chiyya.bio: A contemporary of Rabbah, Rav Yosef became the head of the academy in Pumpedita after Rabbah's death. He was known for his humility and for his mastery of the corpus of Jewish law. While wealthy, Rav Yosef had health issues which brought him blindness and the loss of memory.

yochanan-ben-bag-bag.bio: Ben Bag Bag was an early scholar who was considered to be very learned.

yochanan-the-high-priest.bio: Yochanan (John Hyrkanus) the High Priest was the son of Shimon the Hasmonean and succeeded him as high priest and political leader. He fought several wars against the Syrian Greeks and local enemies. Among them were the Idumeans whom he forced to convert. Though loyal to the Pharisees most of his life, he was finally seduced into joining with the Sadducees.

yose-b-yochanan.bio: Yose b. Yoezer and Yose b. Yochanan served as the first of the zugot (pairs), with the first being Nasi (religious leader) and the second the head of the court. They served after Antigonos in a period of intense Hellenization and war, and promulgated several leniencies to encourage Jews to keep the law under these difficult conditions.

rabbi-yose-b-kisma.bio: A moderate scholar who lived during the Hadrianic persecutions, R Yose b. Kisma advocated accomodation with the Romans.

rav-kahana-(ii).bio: Rav Kahana was an important student of Rav in Babylonia. He executed another Jew based on Jewish law, and hence had to flee to Israel. He then studied with R. Yochanan, who voiced his great admiration for him after initially misjudging him and thinking that he was disrespectful.

rabbi-yosef-hakohen.bio: Rabbi Yosef HaKohen was a Tanna, sage, and priest in the time of the Second Temple. He is cited in rabbinic literature, and several laws of priesthood, ritual purity, and mourning are derived from his name and deeds.

rabbi-yochanan-b-ha-chorani.bio: Rabbi Yochanan b. ha-Chorani was a Tanna who lived in the generation between the era of the Pairs and the era of the Tannaim. He was a student of Shammai the Elder, yet in practice he followed the rulings of Beit Hillel all his life. He was the teacher of Rabbi Elazar b. Rabbi Zadok. The accepted view is that his name indicates that he or one of his parents dwelt in the city of Choran in Syria, though some claim he lived in Beit Choron.

rabbi-abba-yosei-b-hanan.bio: Rabbi Abba Yosei b. Hanan was a second-generation Tanna. Numerous teachings of his are cited in the literature of the Sages.

rabbi-yochanan-b-gudgada.bio: Rabbi Yochanan b. Gudgada was a Levite sage of the first generation of Tannaim. He served in the Second Temple and was among the Levites appointed to lock its gates.

aliases: Rabbi Abba Yosei Chalikuferi of Tivon
rabbi-abba-yosei-chalikuferi.bio: Rabbi Abba Yosei Chalikuferi was a Tanna who likely lived in the generation of the Destruction. He came from the ancient settlement of Tivon in the Lower Galilee. He is mentioned only once in the Mishnah, in connection with a law of impurity that Rabbi Yehoshua transmitted in his name.

rabbi-yosei-ha-kohen.bio: Rabbi Yosei ha-Kohen was a second-generation Tanna of the late first century CE and a student of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. The Mishnah calls him a hasid, a title his teacher and peers used; some identify him with Rabbi Yosei Ketanta. His halachic statements appear only once in the Mishnah, an absence attributed to hasidic humility. The Babylonian Talmud records that he studied Ma'aseh Merkavah with Rabbi Yehoshua and that Rabban Yochanan praised his knowledge of hidden wisdom. It also notes that his handwriting was never held by a non-Jew due to Sabbath caution. He appears in aggadic contexts interpreting verses before Rabban Gamliel, answering his teacher's ethical questions about neighbors, and comforting Rabban Yochanan upon the death of his son. The Chida and Isaac Abarbanel later id

rabbi-yochanan-b-torta.bio: Rabbi Yochanan b. Torta was a third-generation Tanna of the early 2nd century CE and a close friend of Rabbi Akiva. He is remembered for opposing Bar Kokhba, notably challenging Rabbi Akiva's messianic application of "A star shall go forth from Jacob" (Numbers 24:17) to him. Only two statements of his are preserved in rabbinic literature. Aggadic tradition associates him with the legend of a Shabbat-observant cow that inspired a gentile's conversion; some versions identify him as the convert who took the name ben Torta ("son of the cow").

rabbi-yosei-b-dormaskit.bio: Rabbi Yosei b. Dormaskit was a Tanna of the third generation of Mishnaic sages. A student of Rabbi Eliezer b. Hyrcanus and a disputant of Rabbi Yehuda, he appears in the Talmud solely as an aggadist. His only halakhic statement, addressing whether the prohibition of orlah applies outside the Land of Israel, is transmitted in the name of his teacher Rabbi Eliezer the Great.

rabbi-yosei-b-kisma.bio: Rabbi Yosei b. Kisma was a Tanna of the third generation. The Gemara records a sharp dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei in a Tiberias synagogue that tore a Torah scroll; Rabbi Yosei b. Kisma predicted the synagogue would become a house of idolatry, which later occurred. His views on Roman decrees were more moderate than those of other sages. He disputed with Rabbi Hanina b. Teradion over public Torah study under Roman ban, and before dying asked to be buried deep to prevent grave desecration. Roman dignitaries attended his burial; upon returning they found Rabbi Hanina b. Teradion teaching Torah publicly and executed him by fire. The Gemara cites his teaching that the Son of David will come after a certain gate falls and is rebuilt repeatedly. He is traditionally buried on Mount

rabbi-eliezer-b-rabbi-yosei-hagelili.bio: Rabbi Eliezer b. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili was a fourth-generation Tanna of the second century CE, after the Bar Kokhba revolt. A sage of Usha and student of Rabbi Akiva, he appears once in the Mishnah but often in beraitot in both Talmuds and midrashim, mostly in aggadah rather than halakhah. He is credited with the beraita of the thirty-two rules of aggadic interpretation, parallel to Rabbi Yishmael's thirteen halakhic rules. He taught that a mitzvah begun by one and completed by another is credited to the one who completes it. The sages, citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar b. Rabbi Shimon, urged careful attention to his aggadic teachings. The Jerusalem Talmud links him to the family of Bnei Senaah of the tribe of Benjamin, though this may be a corrupted reading. He was buried n

rabbi-yochanan-b-beroka.bio: Rabbi Yochanan b. Beroka was a third-generation Tanna and student of Rabbi Yehoshua b. Hananiah, and a colleague of Rabbi Elazar b. Hisma. Several laws in the Mishnah and many baraitot are cited in his name, often together with Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon. His statement in Avot concerns desecration of God's name. He innovated a ruling that one may redirect an inheritance among heirs of the same gender category fit to inherit, and the halakha follows his opinion. He also ruled that a man must allot provisions for his daughters after his death. Distinctively, he held that the commandment of procreation applies to women as well as men, based on the word "them" in the biblical verse. His son, Rabbi Yishmael, was also a sage whose teachings appear in Avot and in baraitot.

rabbi-yosei-ben-ha-chotef-efrati.bio: Rabbi Yosei ben ha-Chotef Efrati was an Eretz Yisraeli tanna of the fourth generation, mentioned once in the Mishnah in tractate Kilayim. The Jerusalem Talmud records that he studied under Rabbi Yishmael at the end of Rabbi Yishmael's life. His father's epithet ha-Chotef ("the snatcher") is explained in a responsum of Rabbi Menachem Azariah of Fano as denoting one who eagerly seized mitzvot in the marketplace; others speculate it referred to a particular incident or to hasty speech. The Jerusalem Talmud also cites a "Yosef Efrati" who served Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, apparently the same figure.

rabbi-hanina-b-rabbi-yosei-hagelili.canonical: Rabbi Hanina b. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
rabbi-hanina-b-rabbi-yosei-hagelili.canonicalHe: רבי חנינא בן רבי יוסי הגלילי
aliases: R. Hanina b. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
Rabbi Hanina ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili

rabbi-hanina-b-rabbi-yosei-hagelili.bio: Rabbi Hanina b. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili was a Tanna of the fourth generation who lived in the second century, in the generation following the Bar Kokhba revolt. He was among the sages of Usha and the son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili. He appears in only two passages in the Gemara: once in a dispute concerning the sanctification of the new moon, and once in a dispute regarding his kids and chickens that he found slaughtered. According to tradition, he is buried in Dalton in the Galilee, near the graves of his father and his brothers Rabbi Eliezer b. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Shmuel b. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

rabbi-huna-kama.bio: Rabbi Huna Kama, also called Rav Huna the First, served as Exilarch in Babylonia during the era of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi in Eretz Yisrael, in the fifth generation of the Tannaim. A descendant of the royal house of King David, he is distinguished from the famous second-generation Babylonian Amora Rav Huna.

rabbi-yosei-b-zimra.bio: Rabbi Yosei b. Zimra was a Tanna and a priest who lived during the transitional period between the Tannaim and the Amoraim.

rabbi-yosei-b-rabbi-yehuda.bio: Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Yehuda was a Tanna of the final generation of Tannaim. The son of Rabbi Yehuda—one of the most frequently cited Tannaim in the Mishnah—and the grandson of Rabbi Elai, he lived in the generation of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. He learned most of his Torah from his father, though the Talmud records him arguing with Rabbi Yehuda in halakhic discussions. He frequently disputes the older generation, including his father's colleagues and students of Rabbi Akiva such as Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, as well as his contemporary Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

rabbi-yosei-b-yehuda-ish-kfar-habavli.canonicalHe: רבי יוסי בר יהודה איש כפר הבבלי

rabbi-yosei-b-yehuda-ish-kfar-habavli.bio: Rabbi Yosei b. Yehuda ish Kfar haBavli was a sage of the fifth generation of Tannaim. He is mentioned once in the Mishnah, in tractate Avot.

rabbi-menachem-b-yosei.bio: Rabbi Menachem b. Yosei was a fifth-generation Tanna, one of five sons of Rabbi Yosei and brother of Rabbi Yishmael b. Rabbi Yosei. He appears only sparingly in baraitot. He is also called Rabbi Menachem-Verdimos. According to Aharon Heiman, he is the unnamed Rabbi Menachem cited in the Mishnah in tractate Yoma.

rabbi-yishmael-b-rabbi-yosei.bio: Rabbi Yishmael b. Rabbi Yosei was a fifth-generation Tanna. The son and preeminent student of Rabbi Yosei, he also studied under Rabbi Yehuda, and in his later years learned Torah from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and ate at his table. He was a colleague of Rabbi Hiyya and the teacher of Rabbi Hanina b. Hama. He had four brothers: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Halafta, Rabbi Avtilus, and Rabbi Menachem. The Talmud records that when Avdan insulted him in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's study hall, he was severely punished from heaven. Rabbi Yishmael was forced by the king to serve as an officer catching thieves; Elijah the Prophet rebuked him for this and instructed him to flee to another city. rabbi-yosei-b-shaul.bio: Rabbi Yosei b. Shaul was a first-generation Eretz Yisraeli Amora.

rabbi-yochanan-dekatzion.bio: Rabbi Yochanan deKatzion, also called deKartzion, was an Eretz Yisraeli Amora whose exact period is unknown, though he likely belonged to the second generation of Amoraim. Shlomo Sirilio, an early commentator on the Jerusalem Talmud, proposed that his name should be read as Rabbi Yochanan deKisaryon, indicating an origin in Caesarea.

rabbi-yosef-b-rabbi-yehoshua-b-levi.canonical: Rabbi Yosef b. Rabbi Yehoshua b. Levi

rabbi-yosef-b-rabbi-yehoshua-b-levi.bio: Rabbi Yosef b. Rabbi Yehoshua b. Levi was a second-generation Eretz Yisrael Amora and the son of the renowned first-generation Amora Rabbi Yehoshua b. Levi. His father served as his teacher; the Talmud in tractate Chullin records that he asked his father a question concerning the laws of tereifot. His mother was likely the daughter of Rabbi Yosei b. Petras. He was known by the epithet "ben Ari" (son of a lion) in honor of his father, as cited in tractate Yoma, where Zeira b. Hama addressed him with this title while recounting his father's remarkable deeds.

rabbi-yosei-ha-glila.bio: Rabbi Yosei ha-Glila was an Eretz Yisrael Amora of the third–fourth generation. He was likely a student of Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina and a colleague of Rabbi Yonah. The Babylonian Talmud recounts that he once carried a lamp on Shabbat in the presence of Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, relying on the view of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina objected to this.

rabbi-yosei-of-yokrat.bio: Rabbi Yosei of Yokrat was a third-generation Amora and teacher of Rabbi Yosei bar Avin. His hometown, Yokrat, is unidentified today. The Talmud recounts three stories about him: two depict extreme piety bordering on harshness toward his children—he cursed his son for ripening figs out of season, and told his beautiful daughter to "return to dust" so men would not sin, prompting his student Rabbi Yosei bar Avin to leave him for Rav Ashi; the third describes a donkey he rented out returning home with its wages. Some modern scholars argue he is not a historical figure, suggesting the tales symbolize the decline of the Eretz Yisrael center.

rabbi-abba-b-kahana.bio: Rabbi Abba b. Kahana was a third-generation Eretz Yisraeli Amora known as a preacher and aggadist. He spent time in Babylonia in the study hall of Rav Chiya b. Ashi, and many believe he was born there; he may have been the son of Rav Kahana. His primary activity was in Eretz Yisrael, where he was a colleague of Rabbi Levi and Rabbi Zeira.

rabbi-yosei-tzidonia.bio: Rabbi Yosei Tzidonia was an Eretz Yisrael Amora of the fourth generation. He was called Tzidonia because he lived in Tzidon or Tel Beit Tzaida. He was a student of Rabbi Yirmeya and reviewed baraitot before him. He transmitted oral teachings in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.

rav-huna-son-of-rav-ika.canonical: Rav Huna son of Rav Ika
aliases: Rav Huna the son of Rav Ika
rav-huna-son-of-rav-ika.bio: Rav Huna son of Rav Ika was a fourth-generation Amora active in both Eretz Yisrael and Babylonia. He studied under Rabbi Abbahu in Eretz Yisrael and was renowned for transmitting his teacher's words with extreme precision; Rav Safra therefore favored his version of a ruling in a debate with Rav Kahana, another of Rabbi Abbahu's students. He later left Eretz Yisrael for Babylonia with Rav Kahana and Rav Safra, where he discussed halakha with Abaye and Rav Papa, who occasionally stayed at his home. His brother was the prominent Amora Rav Acha son of Rav Ika, frequently cited in the Talmud, often in debate with Rav Papa. He is also known as Rav Huna bar Manoach, and his brothers included Rav Idi and Rav Nahman (or Rav Hinena) son of Rav Ika.

rabbi-yosei-berabbi-bun.bio: Rabbi Yosei beRabbi Bun (called Rabbi Yosei b. Avin in the Babylonian Talmud) was a fourth-generation Eretz Yisraeli Amora of the late fourth century CE. He appears primarily in the Jerusalem Talmud, where he is among the most frequently cited Amoraim, and only rarely in the Babylonian Talmud. He was a student of Rabbi Yosei of Yokrat, and according to Aharon Heiman his father was the Amora Rabbi Avin. In the Jerusalem Talmud he often debates halakha with Rabbi Mana and his students, and his statements typically conclude the sugya. He emended or explained traditions from Rabbi Yochanan and brought Babylonian traditions. He is traditionally credited with editing the Jerusalem Talmud, paralleling Rav Ashi's editing of the Babylonian Talmud. Later Eretz Yisraeli Amoraim are not mentioned by n

rabbi-yosei-bar-zevida.bio: Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida was a fourth-generation Eretz Yisrael Amora. He appears frequently in both Talmuds in disputes with his colleague Rabbi Yona, and in the Jerusalem Talmud he is sometimes called Rabbi Yasa. A student of Rabbi Ila and Rabbi Zeira, he taught first in Rabbi Ila's yeshiva and later in his own, and was one of the closers of the sugyot in tractate Nezikin in the Jerusalem Talmud. He lived in Tiberias; when decrees increased in Eretz Yisrael he briefly descended to Babylonia with Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Bun, then returned to become the leading sage of his generation. All fifth-generation Eretz Yisrael Amoraim were his students, foremost among them Rabbi Mana, and his son was Rabbi Elazar b. Rabbi Yosei.

rav-yosef-b-abba.bio: Rav Yosef b. Abba was a Babylonian Amora who studied under Rabbi Yochanan, Shmuel, and Rav Yehuda. He is mentioned several times in the Talmud, including in a discussion on validating documents in the absence of a litigant, where he explains Rabbi Yochanan’s reasoning by deriving from the verse “and it be testified to its owner” that no legal judgment may be validated without the litigant’s presence. He was a contemporary of Rabba bar Yirmeya, and the Talmud records a joint discussion they held when Rabba bar Yirmeya came to his city.

rav-dimi-b-yosef.bio: Rav Dimi b. Yosef was a third-generation Babylonian Amora. He may be identical to the Rav Dimi who appears throughout the Gemara without any additional appellation.

rav-huna-bar-hiyya.bio: Rav Huna bar Hiyya was a third-generation Babylonian Amora. Most of his Talmudic statements are cited in the name of his teachers, and he appears in the Jerusalem Talmud as well. He studied with Shmuel, Rav Kahana, Rav Nachman, and was among the younger students of Rav Yehuda. He married the daughter of Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba, from whom he received traditions; his son was Levi. After Rav Yehuda’s death, he served as head of the Pumbedita yeshiva when Rabbah declined the post, holding it until his death so that Torah study would not cease. He briefly served as a royal tax collector; upon hearing that the sages objected, he resigned. Rabbah ruled that he remained trustworthy, while Rav Yosef disagreed. He transmitted teachings in the name of Shmuel, and his son Levi was a colleague of Rava ba

rav-yosef-b-hama.bio: Rav Yosef b. Hama was a Babylonian Amora of the third generation who lived in Mechoza. He was a student of Rav Sheshet, though some of his statements in the Talmud are also cited in the name of Rav Nachman bar Yaakov. His son was Rava, a leading Amora and head of the Pumbedita Yeshiva in Mechoza.

rav-kahana-of-pum-nahara.bio: Rav Kahana of Pum Nahara was a Babylonian Amora of the third and fourth generations who headed the yeshiva in Pum Nahara. A kohen of Eli's family, he studied with Rav Yehuda and later with Rava, learning Sanhedrin alongside Rav Safra. He emigrated to Eretz Yisrael with Rav Safra and studied with Rabbi Zeira, Rabbi Abbahu, and Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, who prayed for his longevity. Returning to Babylonia, he established his yeshiva in Pum Nahara, where Rav Ashi became his outstanding student; Rav Ashi honored him beyond Amemar. He was a colleague of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, and together they rebuked arrogant wealthy men who interfered in judicial appointments. rav-aha-b-yosef.bio: Rav Aha b. Yosef was a Babylonian Amora of the fourth generation. A leading student of Rav Huna, he also studied under Rav Chisda and was the uncle of Rav Nachman b. Yitzchak. Heiman, author of Seder HaDorot, argued that he was mistakenly conflated with Rav Acha brei d'Rav Yosef, a figure from a different period, while other scholars maintain that the two names refer to the same person.

rav-huna-b-hinena.bio: Rav Huna b. Hinena was a fourth-generation Babylonian Amora.

rav-acha-bar-huna.bio: Rav Acha bar Huna was a fourth-generation Babylonian Amora. He studied under Rav Sheshet in his youth, and after Rav Sheshet’s death he likely studied alongside Rav Shmuel, son of Rabba bar bar Chana, while maintaining contact with Rav Yosef, to whom he sent halakhic inquiries. After Rabba’s death he joined Rava’s academy; Rava treated him as a disciple, assigning him tasks together with Rav Safra. On one occasion Rava sent Rav Acha bar Huna and Rav Safra to offer a sacrifice brought by Ifra Hormiz, mother of King Shapur, instructing them to find untouched ground, unused wood, and kindle fire from stones. He likely served as a judge.

rav-huna-b-yehuda.bio: Rav Huna b. Yehuda was a Babylonian Amora and student of Rav Yehuda and Rav Sheshet, cited often in the Talmud. He was a colleague of Rava; both studied under Rav Sheshet and debated his rulings. They disagreed, for example, regarding a rebellious wife: Rava held their teacher required gradual persuasion with a weekly deduction of seven dinars from her ketubah, whereas Rav Huna maintained that after four weeks she forfeits the entire sum. Rava sometimes stayed at his home; the Talmud relates that on one Shabbat evening Rava recited the blessing over spices before fire at Havdalah, citing Rabbi Yehuda's version of the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Scholars such as Ze'ev Yavetz identify him with Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehuda.

aliases: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
rav-huna-b-rav-yehoshua.bio: Rav Huna b. Rav Yehoshua was a fifth-generation Babylonian Amora and one of its most prominent figures. He studied under Abaye and Rava at the yeshiva of Pumbedita, and was a close colleague and disputant of Rav Papa. When Rav Papa founded the yeshiva in Naresh, Rav Huna joined him and served as rosh kallah, delivering lectures during the months of Adar and Elul. Early in his studies he supported himself from a small parcel of land; later he entered a business partnership with Rav Papa selling sesame. He was known for his humility and willingness to forgo his rights. Once, when he fell ill and Rav Papa prepared shrouds for him, he recovered and taught that because he had always been forgiving, God forgave him as well. He died around 411 CE according to some chronologies, though others sugg

rav-yosef-b-ami.bio: Rav Yosef b. Ami was a Babylonian Amora of the fifth generation. He is mentioned only twice in the Talmud, in one instance raising a contradiction between two statements of Rava. The author of Erech Tannaim veAmoraim infers from this that he belonged to the later generations, and hypothesizes that he may have been the brother of Rav Pinchas b. Ami; if so, he lived in the time of Rav Ashi.

rav-huna-b-natan.bio: Rav Huna b. Natan was a Babylonian Amora of the fifth and sixth generations who served as Exilarch and political head of the Jews in Babylonia. A scion of the Exilarch family descended from King David, he studied under Rav Papa and Amemar and sat before Rava in the yeshiva. His tenure as Exilarch coincided with Rav Ashi's leadership of the Sura academy. He enjoyed close ties with the Sassanian king Yazdegerd I, who ruled Babylonia and favored the Jews, and was a member of the royal household. Some scholars distinguish between two figures: Huna b. Natan of the sixth generation and Rav Huna b. Natan of the fourth and fifth generations.

rav-huna-b-manoach.bio: Rav Huna b. Manoach was a Babylonian Amora of the sixth generation. After studying under Rava, he went together with Rav Shmuel b. Idi and Rav Chiyya of Vestaniya to study under Rav Papa, who headed the yeshiva. He and his colleagues were dissatisfied with Rav Papa's study method; when his teachings displeased them they would hint to each other, offending Rav Papa. Rav Papa dreamed a heavenly warning that severe punishment might befall these three students, alluding to the verse "And I will cut off the three shepherds." Following the dream, Rav Papa asked them to leave his beit midrash, and they departed. Rav Huna b. Manoach transmits many statements in the name of Rav Acha b. Rav Ika.

aliases: Rav Nehemiah son of Rav Yosef
R. Nehemiah son of Rav Yosef
rav-nehemiah-b-rav-yosef.bio: Rav Nehemiah b. Rav Yosef was a sixth-generation Babylonian Amora and the son of Rav Yosef, head of the Pumbedita academy. Born late in his father's life, few statements are cited in his name. He was an expert in examining tereifot, particularly lung adhesions (sircha), and developed independent methods for their inspection. A distinguished student of Rava, he learned from both his revealed and hidden conduct, including a ruling about sharpening a knife on a festival with a change (shinui) and a lesson that one should prioritize guarding tefillin even at slight cost to their honor. Later Amoraim labored to understand his rulings. He served as head of the court in his city and was a colleague of Rav Papa, Rav Papi, and Rav Huna b. Rav Yehoshua.

rav-nachman-b-rav-huna.bio: Rav Nachman b. Rav Huna was one of the last Babylonian Amoraim and head of the Sura academy. According to Rav Sherira Gaon's letter, he succeeded Rav Idi b. Avin as head of Sura in 451 CE and led the academy for three years until his death in 454 CE. He is not mentioned in the Talmud by his full name; some scholars identify him with a Rav Nachman who debated with Rav Ashi and Ravina, though Shalom Albeck maintains that these passages require emendation and that he is absent from the Talmud entirely. He was not the son of the earlier Amora Rav Huna, and no connection between them is known. A tradition in Shibolei ha-Leket links his days to the institution of embedding the Shema within Kedushah to evade a Persian decree, though some emend the text to place that decree after his death.

rav-yosef-b-rava.bio: Rav Yosef b. Rava was a Babylonian Amora, the son of Rava and a student of Rav Yosef. Ketubot 63a:3 describes his father sending him to study with Rav Yosef for a planned six years. He returned after three years to see his household. In Eruvin 82b:17, Rav Yosef asks him about his father’s opinion. In Yevamot 64b:21, he asks Rava to explain answers he received from Rav Yosef. His exact generation remains uncertain.

rav-avina-bar-rav-huna.bio: Rav Avina bar Rav Huna, known as Ravina the Last, was a Babylonian Amora of the eighth and final generation. He succeeded his teacher Rabba Tosfa'ah as head of the yeshiva in Mata Mehasia, a suburb of Sura. He completed the editing of the Babylonian Talmud begun by Rav Ashi and Ravina the First, sealing the teachings of earlier generations shortly before his death in 499. His death marked the end of the Amoraic period of hora'ah. The Talmudic statement "Rav Ashi and Ravina are the end of hora'ah" (Bava Metzia 86a) was applied by Rav Sherira Gaon to Rav Ashi and to him as the one who sealed the Talmud. Subsequent sages, including some of his students, were known as the Savoraim, who explained the Gemara.

rav-huna-gaon.bio: Rav Huna Gaon was among the first heads of the Sura yeshiva. He served as Gaon following the death of Rav Chanina Gaon in 640 for about ten years. Some opinions regard him as one of the Savoraim. Some of his statements appear in the Babylonian Talmud, and he is credited by some with composing the first sugya in Tractate Kiddushin. He died in 650 and was succeeded by Rav Sheshna Gaon.

mar-b-rav-huna.bio: Mar b. Rav Huna (died c. 614 or 620) was a leading figure of the third generation of Savoraim in the seventh century and head of the Sura Academy in Babylonia during the late Sasanian Empire. He reopened the Sura academy after it had been inactive for over fifty years due to persecutions and pogroms against the Jews of Babylonia in the Savoraic period. According to another view, based on the Iggeret of Rav Sherira Gaon, he is regarded as the first of the Geonim of Sura.

rabbah-yosei.bio: Rabbah Yosei was among the last Babylonian Amoraim and the first generation of Savoraim in the fifth century. He headed the Pumbedita academy from 476 until his death in 514. He assisted Ravina in completing the first stage of the Babylonian Talmud's redaction, and under his leadership the Savoraic editing of the Talmud began, consisting mainly of explanations, completions, and halakhic rulings.

abba-yose-ben-dostai.bio: Abba Yose ben Dostai was a relatively obscure Palestinian tanna of the second century CE who is not cited in the Mishnah itself but appears in the Tosefta, baraitot and tannaitic midrashim. He transmitted halakhic statements in the names of the earlier tannaim Rabbi Eliezer (ben Hyrcanus) and Rabbi Yose ha-Gelili, which places him a generation or so after them, and he was a contemporary of Yose ben Meshullam, with whom several of his halakhot are quoted jointly. Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi cites aggadot in his name dealing with the reconciliation of apparently contradictory biblical verses, a hallmark of his preserved teaching. His surviving material is mostly halakhic rulings scattered through the Tosefta (e.g. Pe'ah 4:2, Ta'anit 2:6, Kelim Bava Metzia 6:18, Makhshirin 2:10) and the Sifrei (Numbers 42), so he is a peripheral but genuine figure of the late tannaitic period.

rabbi-yochanan-ben-dahavai.bio: Yochanan ben Dahavai was a tanna of the land of Israel who does not appear in the Mishnah but is cited in several baraitot across the Bavli, Tosefta, and Sifra. He transmits halakhot in the name of Rabbi Yehuda (bar Ilai) — most prominently the ruling that a person blind in one eye is exempt from the pilgrimage obligation of 're'iyah' (appearance at the Temple), derived from reading the verse 'yera'eh/yir'eh' (Exodus 23:17) as requiring two-way seeing (Chagigah 2a, 4b; Arakhin 2b; Tosefta Chagigah 1:2; Sanhedrin 4b, where the source is given as Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima). The Tosefta records that Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) responded against his view and that the Sages decided in favor of Rabbi Yehuda's position. He also gives an opinion on the dyeing of tekhelet (Menachot 42b) and a related exegesis of 'shni tola'at' (Sifra, Metzora 1), and is the author of the rejected teaching in Nedarim 20a on marital conduct. The name 'Dahavai' (from Aramaic 'dahava', gold) is widely regarded as an epithet rather than a birth name, perhaps reflecting a goldsmith father or a wordplay on one of his teachings (R. Reuven Margaliot, Shemot ve-Kinuyim ba-Talmud).

abba-yose-ben-dostai-2.bio: Abba Yose ben Dostai was a Palestinian tanna of the second century CE, both a halakhist and an aggadist, though he is never cited in the Mishnah. He transmitted halakhic statements in the names of the earlier sages R. Eliezer (ben Hyrcanus) and R. Yose ha-Gelili (Tosefta Pe'ah 4:2; Ta'anit 2:6), which marks him as a tanna of the third generation. He was a contemporary of Yose ben Meshullam, with whom several halakhot are jointly quoted (Tosefta Kelim Bava Metzia 6:18; Makhshirin 2:10). His aggadot — most famously his reconciliations of apparently contradictory biblical verses — were largely preserved and transmitted by R. Judah ha-Nasi (Rebbi) himself (e.g., Sifrei Numbers 42, Numbers Rabbah 11:19). A demonological tale told of him appears with him as the hero ('Abba Yose ben Dositai') in Midrash Tehillim to Psalm 20:7, while parallels in Leviticus Rabbah 24:3 and Tanhuma Kedoshim 9 attach the story to 'Yose of Zitor.'
